content:
Even if mathlib, batteries, and core don't have any interest in being backwards compatible right now, I believe that Lean should be designed in a way that allows library writers to make their own libraries completely backwards compatible.

But right now, it seems that you can't really add new definitions in a backwards compatible way, because of the open command. Suppose library A wants to add a new definition, so for backwards compatibility, they add it as A.x. This prevents conflicts with any x that might have been added in a downstream library. But if this downstream library had opened A, the namespace doesn't really do anything any more and we have a conflict again.

-- Upstream library
def A.x := 1 -- new (breaking) change

-- Downstream library
def B.x := 2 -- already existed for a while
open A B
#eval x -- Ambiguous term x

I noticed that functions like docs#List.append and docs#Array.append were marked as protected, as if in anticipation that some user might try to open both namespaces. One solution to this problem is to mark all new definitions as protected, so that once you have established a public API you can never add anything non-protected to it.

Another solution is to just never use the open command. That is, downstream libraries must not open anything if they want to benefit from backwards compatibility. This is pretty much standard practice in C++. There could also be an analog of Python's import ... as .... But we use the open command for all sorts of things like notation, so getting rid of open has other problems.

Which of these solutions is better? Alternatively, is there another solution?
Related thread: #mathlib4 > Rename lim to Filter.lim?

How about

-- Upstream library
def A.x := 1 -- new (breaking) change

-- Downstream library
def B.x := 2 -- already existed for a while
open A hiding x
open B
#eval x -- Unambiguous
This still requires a change to be made in the downstream library in response to a change in the upstream library, which is what I am hoping to avoid.

Then using restricted open in your downstream library would work. That is open A (foo bar baz). It's good hygiene to only import the things you need and any new declaration upstream will not affect your code.
